questions.question: How does HashMap work internally in Java?
questions.title: HashMap Internals
questions.direct_answer: HashMap uses an array of buckets; keys are hashed to find a bucket index, and collisions are handled by a linked list (treeified to a red-black tree at 8+ entries in Java 8+).

interviewer_intent.testing: The most frequently asked Java internals question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Stopping at 'it uses hashing' without explaining collision handling, load factor, or Java 8 treeification
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the full flow: hashCode → index → bucket → collision → treeify, plus why equals/hashCode contract matters

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So HashMap internally uses an array of buckets — by default 16 buckets. When you put a key-value pair:

1. Java calls `key.hashCode()` to get an integer.
2. It applies a hash function to map that integer to an array index (0-15 for default capacity).
3. The pair is stored at that index (bucket).

When two keys hash to the same bucket — a collision — Java handles it with a linked list at that bucket. So get() on a collided bucket is O(n) in the worst case.

Java 8 improvement: when a single bucket accumulates 8 or more entries, the linked list is converted to a red-black tree (O(log n) lookup). When entries drop below 6, it converts back to a linked list.

Load factor (default 0.75) controls when the array resizes. When entries > capacity × 0.75, HashMap doubles its capacity and rehashes everything. This is expensive, so choose initial capacity wisely if you know the size upfront.

The equals/hashCode contract is critical: if two objects are equal (a.equals(b)), they MUST have the same hashCode. If you violate this, you can't find a key you put in.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Default 16 buckets, load factor 0.75
hashCode() → bucket index
Collision: linked list (Java 8: treeify at 8 entries → O(log n))
Resize: when entries > capacity × 0.75 (doubles and rehashes)
equals/hashCode contract: equal objects must have equal hashCodes

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: a library filing system with labeled shelves

speakable_v2.hook: HashMap is just an array of buckets — hashing tells you which bucket, and a chain handles the rare collision.

beats.text: HashMap stores key-value pairs in an array of buckets (16 by default). To put an entry, Java calls hashCode() on the key, maps that integer to an array index, and stores the pair there. To get a value, Java hashes the key again, goes to that bucket, and uses equals() to find the exact match. Average case is O(1) for both operations.

The bucket-array design makes key lookup constant time on average. Without hashing, finding a key in a collection of n entries would require scanning all n — that's O(n). Hashing maps any key directly to a position in a fixed-size array.

items: hashCode() step: computes an integer from the key, then maps it to a bucket index between 0 and capacity-1.
Collision handling: two keys landing in the same bucket form a linked list. Java 8 converts that list to a red-black tree when one bucket reaches 8 entries — worst case drops from O(n) to O(log n).
Load factor (default 0.75): when entries / capacity exceeds 0.75, the array doubles and all entries are rehashed — expensive but infrequent.
equals/hashCode contract: equal objects must have equal hashCodes — breaking this causes put entries to be 'lost' on get.

beats.text: production trap: in the product catalog app you use a custom Product as a HashMap key. You override equals() to compare by productId but forget to override hashCode(). Two equal Product objects hash to different buckets. You put one in the map and call get() with an equal-but-different Product instance — you get null. The entry is in the map but unreachable.

items: Always override both equals() and hashCode() together when using custom objects as keys — overriding only equals() breaks the lookup.
Pre-size the map if you know the entry count: new HashMap<>(expectedSize * 4/3 + 1) avoids expensive resize operations.

speakable_v2.cap: Know the five steps: hashCode → bucket index → store/retrieve → collision chain → treeify at 8 — that's the complete HashMap story.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap, Hashtable, and ConcurrentHashMap?
questions.title: HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap
questions.direct_answer: HashMap is not thread-safe; Hashtable is synchronized but slow (deprecated); ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe with segment-level locking for better concurrent performance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Thread safety awareness and legacy API knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending Hashtable for thread-safe use — ConcurrentHashMap is the correct answer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain WHY ConcurrentHashMap is better (segment/bucket-level locking vs full lock)

seo.metaDescription: Complete comparison of HashMap, Hashtable, and ConcurrentHashMap — thread safety, performance, and when to use each.

familiarity_anchors: a single-user spreadsheet vs a shared Google Sheet

speakable_v2.hook: Hashtable is the heavy padlock from 1996 — ConcurrentHashMap is the modern fine-grained lock that actually scales.

groups.heading: HashMap
groups.text: Not thread-safe — fastest in single-threaded code. Allows one null key and multiple null values. Iterators are fail-fast (throw ConcurrentModificationException if the map changes during iteration).

groups.heading: Hashtable
groups.text: Legacy Java 1.0 class. Synchronizes every method with a single lock — safe but very slow under concurrency. No nulls allowed. Avoid in new code.

items: Use HashMap for single-threaded code or when you control synchronization externally.
Use ConcurrentHashMap for multi-threaded access — it locks at the bucket level, so multiple threads can read and write different buckets simultaneously.
Never recommend Hashtable — ConcurrentHashMap is always the better thread-safe choice.

beats.text: sharp edge: ConcurrentHashMap doesn't allow null keys or values by design. When map.get(key) returns null, it unambiguously means the key is absent — not that the key maps to null. This removes the ambiguity that would be dangerous in concurrent code where you can't atomically check-then-get.

speakable_v2.cap: Single-threaded: HashMap. Multi-threaded: ConcurrentHashMap. Hashtable: never in new code.

questions.question: Can HashMap have null keys and null values?
questions.title: HashMap Null Keys/Values
questions.direct_answer: HashMap allows one null key (stored in bucket 0) and multiple null values; TreeMap and Hashtable do not allow null keys.

interviewer_intent.testing: Edge case knowledge of Map implementations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking HashMap doesn't allow nulls, or not knowing TreeMap throws NullPointerException on null keys
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why null key works (HashMap handles it specially at bucket 0) and why TreeMap can't (needs compareTo)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So HashMap is one of the few Map implementations that handles null gracefully. It allows exactly one null key — internally, null keys are stored in bucket 0 without calling hashCode(). It also allows any number of null values — `map.put("key", null)` is valid.

TreeMap does NOT allow null keys because it needs to call compareTo() on keys for sorting — and null.compareTo() throws NullPointerException. TreeMap does allow null values though.

Hashtable (legacy) allows neither null keys nor null values.

ConcurrentHashMap allows neither null keys nor null values — this was a deliberate design decision to avoid ambiguity: `map.get(key)` returning null could mean 'key not present' or 'key maps to null', which is problematic in concurrent code.

sections.title: Key Points
content: HashMap: 1 null key + multiple null values ✓
TreeMap: no null keys (compareTo fails), null values ok
Hashtable: no nulls at all
ConcurrentHashMap: no nulls at all
Check with containsKey() vs get() to distinguish null-value vs missing key

familiarity_anchors: a form that accepts a blank field vs one that requires input
an optional label on a box

speakable_v2.hook: HashMap is the one Map that gracefully handles null keys — but TreeMap and ConcurrentHashMap both reject them for different reasons.

beats.text: HashMap allows one null key (stored in bucket 0 without calling hashCode) and any number of null values. TreeMap rejects null keys because it calls compareTo() on keys for sorting — calling compareTo on null throws NullPointerException. ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values by design to avoid ambiguity in concurrent reads.

HashMap's null key support is a deliberate design choice — it covers the case where a key is optional or unknown. TreeMap and ConcurrentHashMap reject null keys because their internals require calling methods on the key that would throw on null.

items: HashMap: 1 null key allowed (bucket 0), unlimited null values allowed.
TreeMap: null key throws NullPointerException (compareTo called on key for sorting); null values are fine.
Hashtable: no null keys, no null values — legacy behavior.
ConcurrentHashMap: no null keys, no null values — ambiguity prevention.

beats.text: non-obvious: in a product catalog app, map.get(productId) returning null could mean two things — the product isn't in the map, or the product is mapped to null. Use containsKey(productId) first to distinguish. In ConcurrentHashMap, null returns unambiguously mean absent, which is why it bans null values entirely.

items: Don't confuse 'key not found' with 'key maps to null' — call containsKey before get when null values are possible.
Switching from HashMap to ConcurrentHashMap will break code that stores null values — a quiet runtime regression.

speakable_v2.cap: Remember: HashMap yes to nulls, TreeMap no null keys, ConcurrentHashMap no nulls at all — and always distinguish absence from a null value with containsKey.

questions.question: What are initial capacity and load factor in HashMap, and how do you choose them?
questions.title: HashMap Capacity and Load Factor
questions.direct_answer: Initial capacity is the number of buckets at creation (default 16); load factor (default 0.75) is the threshold ratio that triggers resizing when exceeded.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that resizing is expensive and can be avoided with a good initial capacity
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the formula: if you know you'll store N entries, set initial capacity to N/0.75 + 1 to avoid any resize

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So HashMap has two performance tuning parameters. Initial capacity is the number of buckets created at startup — default 16. Load factor (default 0.75) determines when to resize: when entries / capacity exceeds the load factor, HashMap doubles its capacity and rehashes all entries.

Resizing is expensive — O(n) operation. If you know you'll store a lot of entries, set initial capacity upfront. For N expected entries: `new HashMap<>(N * 4/3 + 1)` — that's N divided by 0.75, rounded up. This avoids any resize.

Lower load factor = fewer collisions, more memory. Higher load factor = more collisions, less memory. The default 0.75 is a well-tested balance.

Practical example: if you're building a frequency map from a 10,000-word text, `new HashMap<>(16000)` avoids resizing. Default capacity would trigger about 9 resizes.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Default: 16 capacity, 0.75 load factor
Resize when: entries > capacity × load factor (expensive!)
Pre-size: new HashMap<>(expectedSize * 4/3 + 1)
Lower load factor = fewer collisions but more memory
Rehashing rehashes all existing entries — avoid by pre-sizing

followup_questions: How do you avoid HashMap resizing?

seo.metaTitle: HashMap Initial Capacity and Load Factor in Java
seo.metaDescription: How initial capacity and load factor affect HashMap performance, resizing cost, and how to pre-size.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: pre-booking a hotel with estimated guests
parking garage that doubles its floors when full
speakable_v2.hook: Load factor is the trigger; initial capacity is the head start — together they control whether your map ever pays for an expensive resize.

beats.text: Initial capacity is the number of buckets HashMap creates at startup — default is 16. Load factor (default 0.75) is the fill threshold: when the number of stored entries exceeds capacity times load factor, HashMap doubles its bucket array and rehashes every entry. That rehash is O(n) and can be avoided entirely by pre-sizing.

The load factor balances collision rate against memory use. A low load factor (say 0.5) keeps buckets sparse — fewer collisions but twice as many empty buckets. A high load factor (say 0.9) packs more entries in — less memory but more collisions per bucket. The default 0.75 is a well-tested sweet spot.

items: Initial capacity: buckets allocated at creation. Doubling on resize means log2(n) resizes for n entries from default.
Load factor 0.75: resize triggers when entries > capacity × 0.75. Default 16 buckets → first resize at entry 13.
Pre-sizing formula: new HashMap<>(N * 4/3 + 1) for N expected entries — zero resizes guaranteed.

beats.text: non-obvious: in the product catalog app, loading 100,000 products into a default HashMap triggers roughly 13 resize-and-rehash cycles. Pre-sizing with new HashMap<>(150000) (100000 divided by 0.75 plus margin) skips all of them. The savings are real in high-throughput startup paths.

items: Don't set load factor to 1.0 hoping to save memory — more collisions per bucket will slow down get/put more than the memory savings are worth.
Pre-sizing only helps when you know the entry count upfront — don't over-engineer it for dynamic-size maps.

speakable_v2.cap: When you know the entry count, pre-size with N * 4/3 + 1 — it eliminates all resize work and costs you nothing in correctness.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of HashMap get() and put() operations?
questions.title: HashMap Time Complexity
questions.direct_answer: O(1) average case for get() and put(); O(n) worst case when all keys collide into one bucket (rare with a good hash function).

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying O(1) without mentioning the worst case or the Java 8 O(log n) treeification improvement
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Java 8 treeification brings worst case to O(log n) for a single bucket

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So HashMap get() and put() are O(1) amortized average case. That's the number interviewers expect. The 'amortized' part means it's O(1) per operation across many operations, excluding occasional O(n) resize events.

Worst case is technically O(n) if every key happens to hash to the same bucket — all entries form one long chain. But a decent hash function makes this extremely unlikely in practice.

Java 8 improvement: when a bucket's chain exceeds 8 entries, it's converted to a red-black tree. This makes the worst-case for a single over-loaded bucket O(log n) instead of O(n).

For iteration: O(capacity + size) — iterates all buckets even if empty, then all entries.

sections.title: Key Points
content: get/put: O(1) average
Worst case: O(n) all keys collide
Java 8 treeify: worst case O(log n) per bucket
Resize: O(n) — rehashes all entries
Iteration: O(capacity + size)

seo.metaTitle: HashMap Time Complexity in Java — O(1) get and put
seo.metaDescription: HashMap time complexity — O(1) average for get/put, worst case, Java 8 treeification, and iteration cost.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: going directly to the right shelf in a library
speakable_v2.hook: HashMap get and put are O(1) on average — but saying just that without the caveats is only half the answer.

beats.text: HashMap get() and put() are O(1) on average — you hash the key to a bucket index in constant time, then check the bucket. Amortized O(1) means that across many operations the average is constant, even though an occasional resize is O(n).

The O(1) guarantee holds because a good hash function spreads keys evenly across buckets. Finding a bucket is a single array index lookup — that's always O(1). Collision chains are kept short, so the bucket scan stays negligible.

items: Average case: O(1) for get and put — hash to bucket, small or empty chain, done.
Worst case (theoretical): O(n) if all keys land in one bucket and form a long chain.
Java 8 improvement: chains beyond 8 entries treeify — worst case per bucket becomes O(log n).
Iteration: O(capacity + size) — even empty buckets are visited.

beats.text: candidates miss: the full answer is O(1) average, O(log n) worst case per bucket in Java 8+, O(n) for a full resize. In the product catalog app, get by product ID is effectively instant for any reasonable catalog size — the hash lookup is constant regardless of whether you have 100 or 100,000 products.

items: Don't say just O(1) — always add 'average case' and mention the Java 8 treeification improvement to stand out.
Don't forget that iteration is O(capacity + size), not O(size) — a large initial capacity with few entries means lots of empty bucket scanning.

speakable_v2.cap: O(1) average, O(log n) worst case per bucket (Java 8+), O(n) for resize — knowing all three shows you actually understand the internals.

questions.question: Why must you override both equals() and hashCode() when using custom objects as HashMap keys?
questions.title: equals() and hashCode() Contract
questions.direct_answer: HashMap uses hashCode() to find the bucket and equals() to confirm the key match — overriding only one breaks the lookup and causes items to be 'lost' in the map.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Object contract — extremely common interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overriding only equals() for domain equality without knowing hashCode() is used for bucket lookup
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the concrete broken scenario: two 'equal' objects → different hashCodes → different buckets → map.get() returns null

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So when you use a custom object as a HashMap key, HashMap calls two methods. First, hashCode() to compute which bucket index to look in. Then equals() to confirm that the key in the bucket is actually equal to your search key.

If you override equals() but not hashCode(), here's what breaks: two objects that are logically equal (equals() returns true) will have different hashCodes (default is based on memory address). They hash to different buckets. So `map.put(key1, value)` puts it in bucket 5, then `map.get(key2)` where key2.equals(key1) is true looks in bucket 17 — finds nothing — returns null. The value is 'lost'.

The contract: if a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). The reverse is not required — two objects can have the same hashCode without being equal (hash collision).

In practice: use IDE generation or Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode. Always override both, never just one.

sections.title: Key Points
content: HashMap uses hashCode() to find bucket, equals() to find exact key
Override only equals() → 'lost' entries in map
Contract: a.equals(b) → a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()
Same hashCode ≠ equal (just a collision)
Use IDE generate or Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode

seo.metaTitle: Why Override equals() and hashCode() for HashMap Keys
seo.metaDescription: The equals() and hashCode() contract for HashMap — what breaks when you override only one, and the correct approach.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: a two-lock safe that needs both keys
a library card catalog with shelf location and title match
speakable_v2.hook: HashMap uses two methods to find a key: hashCode picks the shelf, equals confirms the book — override only one and your data is permanently lost.

beats.text: HashMap retrieves a value in two steps: first it calls hashCode() on the lookup key to compute which bucket to check, then it calls equals() on each key in that bucket to find the exact match. Both methods must work correctly for lookups to succeed. If they're inconsistent, entries become unreachable.

The two-step design lets HashMap be fast. HashCode narrows the search to one of thousands of buckets. Equals then confirms within that small bucket. Both steps are necessary — neither alone is sufficient.

items: The contract: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode().
Reverse is NOT required: two objects can share a hashCode (collision) without being equal.
Default hashCode() is based on memory address — two logically equal objects in different memory locations return different hashCodes.

beats.text: production trap: in the product catalog app, Product overrides equals() to compare by productId but doesn't override hashCode(). Two Product objects with the same productId are logically equal. map.put(product1, price) stores it in bucket 5 (product1's memory address). map.get(product2) hashes to bucket 17 (product2's different address) — returns null. The entry exists in the map but can never be found.

items: Overriding only equals() is the most common custom-object-as-key mistake — entries go in but never come out.
Use your IDE's generate equals/hashCode, or add Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode — writing them manually is error-prone.

speakable_v2.cap: Always override both equals and hashCode together — they're a pair, and HashMap requires both to locate any key correctly.
